title: Nvidia Investigates CEO's Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy
paragraphs: Nvidia's board of directors has launched an independent investigation into the company's chief executive, Jensen Huang, following reports that he may have been the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

The board announced the inquiry on Sunday, November 8, saying it was responding to recent reporting that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The investigation will be overseen by independent directors with the help of outside legal counsel. Huang, 63, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it ever since, will remain in his role while the inquiry takes place.

The allegations first surfaced in October, when The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had concluded that a woman named Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. She is a Chinese citizen and a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that has become one of Nvidia's largest customers. According to the newspaper, Megaspeed purchased around $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years. Despite sharing a surname, she is not related to the Nvidia CEO.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged to the board that he had an intimate relationship with a business executive. In a message to employees reported by The New York Times, he wrote that he had been unfaithful to his wife and that his actions had hurt her and their children, adding that he was "deeply sorry."

The board stated that it had "no reason to believe" that US national security or Nvidia's confidential information had been compromised, but said its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang has said he supports the investigation and will cooperate fully.

The case has attracted attention in Washington because Nvidia's most advanced chips, which power artificial intelligence data centers, are subject to US export restrictions designed to keep them out of China. Three Republican House committee leaders have invited Huang to a closed-door briefing on espionage risks. Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry dismissed the accusation as unsubstantiated and described it as a smear against China.
It is important to note that the spy allegations are based on press reports citing unnamed intelligence sources, and they have not been proven.
